title: Schopenhauer
keyWorks: The World as Will and Representation (1819)
Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life (1851)
summary: Arthur Schopenhauer was a German philosopher who believed that at the root of everything lies a blind, insatiable “will” — an endless striving that is never finally satisfied. Hence his famous pessimism. But he also found ways out: compassion, art and quiet contemplation, in which the will falls silent for a while.
onEmotions: For Schopenhauer, feelings are how the will feels from the inside: desire, lack, fear of loss, brief relief. He considered suffering not a mistake or a personal failure but the basic fabric of life — so there is nothing shameful in it. Relief comes not from fulfilling every desire (that is impossible) but from moments when we stop only wanting and begin to look: in music, in nature, in art. And the understanding that others suffer just as we do gives rise to compassion — for Schopenhauer, the basis of all morality.

anxiety.text: Every night Schopenhauer laid loaded pistols beside his bed: the philosopher of the will knew firsthand how it gives no rest. If everything inside you is braced for trouble, he would understand without explanation. Schopenhauer described the human being as a manifestation of the “will” — a blind striving that constantly reaches forward into the future and is always afraid of something. So anxiety is not a malfunction but the voice of the will itself, which doesn't know how to settle down. Schopenhauer advised not arguing with this restless striving head-on but stepping out of it from time to time. He called this “aesthetic contemplation”: when you truly look at a cloud or a tree, or listen to music, for a moment you stop being the one who wants and fears and become simply the one who sees. Anxiety doesn't vanish for good, but it gets a respite — and you discover that there is more in you than anxiety.
anxiety.practice: Try what Schopenhauer called contemplation: pick a cloud, a branch or a crack in the wall and look at it for a minute as if you needed nothing from it. The anxiety may stay — just notice that the one who is looking is calmer.

fear.text: In 1831, when cholera reached Berlin, Schopenhauer left for Frankfurt at once. Europe's great pessimist saved his life without a moment's hesitation — and if you are afraid right now, your body is doing the same thing. Schopenhauer believed that everything alive is pervaded by the “will to live” — an unconscious striving to exist and preserve oneself. Fear, in Schopenhauer's view, is its most direct expression: the will protects itself before we've even had time to think. So there's no sense in scolding yourself for being afraid — fear is older than your character and your decisions. Schopenhauer distinguished the will from “representation” — our ability to see the world as a picture. When you can describe your fear in words, as if examining it from the outside, you partly cross over from will into representation. The fear remains, but it stops being your whole world: someone appears who is looking at it.
fear.practice: Put a hand on your chest and feel your heart beating: this is the will to live made visible. Tell it silently, “I hear you, you're protecting me,” and take three out-breaths longer than the in-breaths.

sadness.text: Above Schopenhauer's desk stood a bust of Kant, and nearby a gilded statue of the Buddha — the teacher who began by saying that life is suffering. This philosopher would never demand cheerfulness from you: he would find your sadness honest. He believed life by its very structure is closer to lack than to fullness: the satisfaction of desires is brief, while desire itself is long. So sadness is not a sign that something is wrong with you but rather a sober perception of how the world is made. There is an unexpected comfort in this: you are not alone in your sorrow; all living beings share it. From this understanding Schopenhauer derived “compassion” — a feeling of shared fate with all who suffer. He also especially valued music: in his view, it expresses the will itself directly, without words, which is why a sad melody can console more deeply than any advice.
sadness.practice: Schopenhauer thought music was the voice of the will itself. Put on a melody that sounds the way your sadness feels and listen to the end, fixing nothing. Let the music say what you can't put into words.

grief.text: “Tat tvam asi” — “that thou art”: Schopenhauer considered this phrase from the Upanishads the highest wisdom humanity knows. When someone in whom you recognized yourself is gone, it hurts as if part of you had gone too, and that grief needs time. Schopenhauer wrote a great deal about transience: everything that comes into being passes away, and this is true of everything we love. He didn't prettify this truth. But his philosophy holds another thought as well: behind individual beings stands a single will, one and the same essence manifesting in each of us. Think this through, and your bond with the one you lost was not an illusion: in love you recognized yourself in the other. Schopenhauer considered such recognition the basis of compassion and the most genuine thing in a human being. Grief is the price of that recognition, and the fact that it hurts speaks of the depth of the bond, not of weakness.
grief.practice: Say quietly, “Tat tvam asi — that thou art,” thinking of the one you lost. Recall one of their traits that lives on in you too, and stay with it, doing nothing.

loneliness.text: “He who does not love solitude does not love freedom,” wrote Schopenhauer, who lived his last thirty years with almost no one close to him. But if you're lonely and hurting right now, he wouldn't lecture you: he knew that silence himself. Schopenhauer — himself a rather lonely man — looked at loneliness in two ways. He noticed that what often draws us to company is not love but boredom and inner emptiness. Hence his parable of the porcupines: in the cold they huddle together, but prick one another with their quills and move apart, until they find a “moderate distance.” On the other hand, he valued solitude as a time when a person can be themselves, without masks. Then loneliness is not a sentence but a search for your own distance: not too far from the warmth, not too close to the quills. And time alone can be not only endured but filled — with a book, music, reflection.
loneliness.practice: Imagine yourself as a porcupine from Schopenhauer's parable on a cold day. Where is your “moderate distance” right now — a little closer to people or a little further? Take one tiny step that way today: a call, a short message or an honest evening alone.

quote.text: A man can be himself only so long as he is alone.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life (1851)

anger.text: Once, in a fit of rage, Schopenhauer shoved a seamstress neighbour off his landing, and a court ordered him to pay her a pension for twenty years. The philosopher of the will knew fury from the inside — and knew that behind anger there is usually something that matters to you. Schopenhauer would explain it as the will colliding with an obstacle: you want something, the world resists, and the will boils over. He also noted that all beings are different manifestations of one and the same will, constantly colliding with one another like hungry creatures in a crowded space. This means the person you're angry with is also gripped by their own will and suffers from it. Schopenhauer didn't call for suppressing anger, but he pointed to a way out through “compassion”: seeing in the other the same tormented being. This doesn't cancel your right to boundaries, but it can loosen anger's grip and give you back your clarity.
anger.practice: Before you act, do what Schopenhauer failed to do on that landing: breathe out and ask yourself what your will wanted and what blocked it. Then ask what the other person wanted, and what they feared.

shame.text: Most of the first edition of The World as Will and Representation ended up as scrap paper, yet Schopenhauer never stopped knowing who he was. When shame burns, it seems that other people's gaze decides everything — and that gaze is exactly what he took apart. Schopenhauer examined closely how much we depend on the opinion of others. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he distinguished what a person is, what a person has, and how a person appears in the eyes of others — and held that we value the last far too highly. In his view, most of our woundedness is tied precisely to others' opinion, which lives only in other people's heads. In Schopenhauer's terms, shame often says more about the power of other people's gaze than about your real worth. Schopenhauer advised shifting the weight from “how I seem” to “what I am”: your inner world, your abilities, your peace of mind.
shame.practice: Imagine a hundred years have passed and no one who saw this moment is still alive. What of you remains in the picture — how you seemed, or what you are? Stay with the second for a minute.

guilt.text: Operari sequitur esse — “action follows from being”: Schopenhauer loved this scholastic formula more than many of his own. If what you did is tormenting you, he would suggest not turning away but looking closely — gently, but honestly. Schopenhauer believed our actions flow from our character, and our character from a will we did not choose. It sounds like an excuse, but he drew a different conclusion: conscience shows us not only a single deed but who we are. Seen this way, guilt is knowledge about yourself, not a verdict. Even more important is his idea of “compassion”: he considered the ability to feel another's pain as your own the basis of morality. If it hurts you that you harmed someone, then compassion is alive in you. And you can turn that same compassion toward yourself: you too are a living being, gripped by the will and capable of making mistakes.
guilt.practice: For Schopenhauer, conscience shows us who we are. Choose one small action that can express today the thing your guilt touched — an apology, a favour, a call — and do it.

envy.text: The young Schopenhauer scheduled his Berlin lectures at the same hour as the famous Hegel — and only a handful of students came. He knew how another's success can burn, so for him envy was not a vice of monsters but a very human thing. Schopenhauer saw it as one of the natural expressions of the will: we measure our well-being not in itself but by comparing it with others'. He noticed that our contentment depends on the ratio between what we want and what we have: as soon as we see in someone else what we lack, the lack suddenly sharpens. In this light, envy is not so much about the other person as about an emptiness in your own desire that has suddenly been lit up. Schopenhauer advised turning your gaze to what you already have, and remembering: someone else's life, seen from outside, looks happier than it is from within. Behind every façade is the same unquenched will.
envy.practice: Imagine you got that other life for one day in full — not the shop window, but all its weekdays, worries and unquenched desires. What of it would you actually want to keep?

emptiness.text: Schopenhauer could gaze at Dutch still lifes — a lemon, a glass, a crust of bread — and thought them the best school of the quiet gaze. Feeling empty, untouched by anything, is frightening; but for him such a pause was not only a misfortune. Schopenhauer described two states of the will: when it wants and doesn't have, that is suffering; when it has obtained, boredom and emptiness set in, because the desire has vanished and a new one hasn't come yet. So emptiness is not a sign that you're “broken” but a natural pause in the will's work. But Schopenhauer also saw an opportunity in such pauses. When desire quiets down, room opens up for “disinterested” contemplation — looking at the world while demanding nothing of it. That is how we look at art and at nature. There's no need to rush to fill the emptiness with a new chase; sometimes it's enough to let your eyes simply rest on something beautiful.
emptiness.practice: Arrange a small still life from whatever is at hand: a cup, an apple, your keys. For a minute look at it like a Dutch painter — light, shadows, curves — wanting nothing from these things.

confusion.text: At twenty-five, having broken off a career in trade, Schopenhauer wrote his dissertation on where our every “because” comes from. When the familiar “becauses” suddenly stop working, feeling lost is an honest response. Schopenhauer opened his main book with the words that the world is our “representation”: everything we know, we know through our own way of seeing — through time, space and causality. It follows that confusion is the moment when you notice that your representation doesn't match what's happening. It's unpleasant, but honest. Schopenhauer also held that behind representation stands the will — what we truly want, often without realizing it. So sometimes confusion clears up not through new reasoning but through a question: what is it that wants something in me, deeper than my thoughts? The answer may not come at once — you can give it time.
confusion.practice: Say two sentences aloud: “I think I should…” and “Somewhere deeper, something in me wants…”. Listen for which one sounds stronger: that is the will behind the representation.

quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: The World as Will and Representation, Vol. 1, § 1 (1819)

fatigue.text: Every day Schopenhauer played the flute — usually Rossini — at the same hour, like clockwork. If your strength is completely gone, he would remind you: this isn't laziness but an honest signal that you've reached your limit. Schopenhauer described life as ceaseless striving: having reached one goal, the will immediately sets the next, and so on without end. In other words, burnout is what happens when for years we live only in “want and achieve” mode, never stepping off the wheel. Schopenhauer compared this state to the wheel of Ixion from Greek myth, which turns without stopping — and wrote that it can be halted for a while by moments of contemplation, when we aren't trying to achieve anything. Rest, in this sense, is not a reward for accomplishments but a right to a respite from the will, one everyone needs.
fatigue.practice: Make your own “Schopenhauer's flute”: hum or whistle one melody from beginning to end without using it for anything. While it sounds, Ixion's wheel stands still.

boredom.text: “Life swings like a pendulum, backwards and forwards, between pain and boredom,” Schopenhauer wrote. Boredom seems a trivial feeling, but for him it is one of the two poles of all human life. Boredom, in his view, is the sensation of the emptiness of existence itself, when the will has nothing to cling to. It sounds bleak, but there's relief in it: boredom is not your personal failure but part of a pendulum all humans share. The best remedy for it, Schopenhauer thought, was not new entertainments but “inner wealth”: interest in thoughts, books, art, observation. A person with a rich inner world, he wrote, depends less on the outer one. Boredom can become an invitation to make yourself a little more at home in that world.
boredom.practice: Go for a short walk, as Schopenhauer did with his poodle — no goal, no headphones. On the way, find one thing that interests you just for itself, bringing you nothing.

quote.text: Life swings like a pendulum backwards and forwards between pain and boredom.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: The World as Will and Representation, Vol. 1, § 57 (1819)

joy.text: Philosophy's most famous pessimist loved Rossini, his poodles and a good dinner. He would not be suspicious of your joy: you can simply give yourself over to it. Still, he considered the satisfaction of desires brief, but he singled out a special kind of joy — the kind that comes in art and contemplation. When you are captured by music, a landscape or the beauty of a moment, you are, in his view, freed for a while from “serving the will”: you don't want, you don't fear, you simply are. He called this the state of the “pure subject of knowing” — the one who only sees. Then the deepest joy is not the one that comes from acquiring something but the one in which you forget yourself. It doesn't need to be held onto or justified. You can simply notice it — and know that you have the capacity for such joy.
joy.practice: Recall the second today when you “forgot yourself” and return to it with your eyes closed: what was before you, what was sounding? Stay there another half-minute — as the “clear eye of the world,” Schopenhauer would say.

love.text: “All true and pure love is compassion,” wrote Schopenhauer — the same man who called falling in love a ruse of nature. If tenderness is overflowing in you right now, his philosophy has a place for it, and a very high one. Schopenhauer wrote about love in two ways. In “The Metaphysics of Sexual Love” he explained falling in love soberly, even harshly, as a ruse of the “will to live,” which strives to continue the species. But he rated another kind of love very highly — love in which you feel another's pain and joy as your own. In his view, in such moments the boundary between “I” and “you” fades, and you recognize in the other the very same essence as in yourself. This means tenderness is neither weakness nor illusion but a moment of insight: you see that the other is not a stranger to you. That, for Schopenhauer, lies at the root of all true kindness.
love.practice: Today, tell one person close to you what you value in them — briefly and directly. Schopenhauer would call it a moment when the boundary between “I” and “you” grows thinner.

quote.text: All true and pure love is compassion.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: The World as Will and Representation, Vol. 1, § 66 (1819)

gratitude.text: After Aristotle, Schopenhauer liked to repeat that the prudent seek not pleasure but freedom from pain. The warm gratitude you feel now he would explain from exactly here — and show why it is so rare. He noticed that we take good things for granted, while we feel lack acutely. Health, peace, loved ones are almost invisible while we have them. In his view, happiness is “negative”: it consists above all in the absence of pain, and so it easily slips past our attention. In Schopenhauer's terms, gratitude is the ability to notice such a quiet good: that nothing hurts right now, that someone is near, that there's warm light in the window. Schopenhauer advised imagining from time to time what it would be like to lose what we have — not to frighten ourselves, but to see the value of what is already ours.
gratitude.practice: Check your body the way Schopenhauer might suggest: what doesn't hurt right now? Teeth, back, head, breathing — silently name each part that is at ease, and thank it.

quote.text: We seldom think of what we have but always of what we lack.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life (1851)

hope.text: Fame came to Schopenhauer when he was over sixty — after three decades in which almost no one read his books. He knew how long one can hold on to hope, and so he spoke of it very soberly. Schopenhauer was wary of hope: he saw that the will constantly promises itself happiness “out there, ahead,” and that this promise is rarely fulfilled the way we imagine. But his thought can be read not as a ban on hope but as advice to aim it more wisely. Seen this way, hope for complete and final happiness makes us vulnerable, while hope for good moments — music, a meeting, kindness, a quiet evening — is entirely realistic. Schopenhauer advised expecting less perfection from life and noticing more of what is possible. Such modest hope doesn't disappoint; it sustains.
hope.practice: Choose one small hope for this week — music, a meeting, a quiet evening — and take one step toward it today: set a time, buy a ticket, send an invitation.

nostalgia.text: Distant mountains look blue and weightless, though up close they are rocks, scree and thorny scrub — Schopenhauer was fond of comparisons like this. If you feel warm and sad about the past right now, there is nothing wrong with it, and he has an explanation. He noticed that in memory the past seems brighter than it really was: the images remain, but the will disappears — the anxieties, desires and worries that tormented us at the time. We remember the past the way one looks at a painting — contemplatively. In this light, nostalgia is partly an “aesthetic” feeling: we long not only for time gone by but also for the freedom from desire that looking from the outside gives us. Which means a similar clarity is available in the present too — if you look at today as a future painting.
nostalgia.practice: Look around as if you were remembering this minute ten years from now: the light, the sounds, the things on the table. Choose one detail you'll want to remember then, and let your gaze rest on it.

craving.text: Schopenhauer compared the satisfaction of a desire to alms thrown to a beggar: it keeps him alive today only to prolong his misery until tomorrow. If there's a sharp “I want it now” inside you, the strength of this craving says nothing bad about you. Schopenhauer would describe it as the “will” in its purest form: a blind striving older than our thoughts and stronger than our decisions. His main observation about the will: satisfaction quenches desire only briefly, and then it returns, often stronger. That's why a craving promises so convincingly that “now it'll feel good” — and so rarely keeps its promise. So the craving is not your voice but the voice of the will sounding through you. You can listen to it like the weather: it rises, peaks and subsides. Schopenhauer would advise not arguing with it head-on but, for a minute, moving from “wanting” into observing — looking at it as a phenomenon of the world.
craving.practice: For five minutes, become a naturalist of the will: note where the craving lives in your body and how strong it is from 1 to 10. After five minutes, measure again — and see how the wave changes on its own.

quote.text: Wealth is like sea-water; the more we drink, the thirstier we become; and the same is true of fame.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life, Ch. 3 (1851)

addiction.text: “Man can do what he wills, but he cannot will what he wills,” Schopenhauer wrote. For someone long caught in the circle of addiction there is relief in this: the fact that getting out is hard is not a moral failure. Schopenhauer would explain this by the very nature of the “will”: it is insatiable, and once it has found a shortcut to relief, it will call you back there again and again. In his essay “On the Freedom of the Will” (1839) he argued that actions follow from character and “motives.” But he also stressed that motives act through knowledge — through what we see and how we see it. When understanding changes, what acts on us changes too. He also spoke of “acquired character” — a calm, honest knowledge of your own strengths and weaknesses, without self-deception and without self-flagellation. It follows that the way out begins not with reproaching yourself but with a clear look: what exactly does this circle give me, and what am I really missing?
addiction.practice: Say aloud or to yourself, “When I reach for this, what I'm really missing is…” — and finish it. If you like, you can say that sentence in front of others too — for example, in a mutual-help group of people who have walked a similar path.

hangover.text: “A healthy beggar is happier than an ailing king,” Schopenhauer wrote in the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life. This morning, when your body aches and shame and scraps of last night pile on top, there is no need to beat yourself up. In the same book he wrote that most of our well-being depends on health, and right now your body is simply making itself felt. And about shame he has a sober observation: we vastly exaggerate the importance of what others think of us — other people's opinions occupy them far less than it seems to us in the night-time replay of memory. In other words, the morning dread is largely the voice of the will, frightened for its place among people. Schopenhauer would suggest not deciding your fate or passing sentence on yourself today, but taking care of your body and letting the day pass.
hangover.practice: Do one simple thing for your body, which for Schopenhauer is simply you: a glass of water, an open window, a slow shower. Then name one fact about last night that you know for certain, apart from the night-time fears.

euphoria.text: What do you do with sudden happiness if you're Europe's most famous pessimist? Schopenhauer's answer was unexpected: enjoy it. And if a bright wave of elation has caught you now, his advice suits you too. Schopenhauer, for all his pessimism, especially prized cheerfulness: in the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he calls it the “ready cash” of happiness — not a promise, but something you have right now. So, he wrote, we should open the door to it whenever it comes, without asking whether it has good reason to be there. At the same time he was honest: such a high is fleeting by nature, like any fulfilment of desire. Think this through, and the wisdom here lies not in holding on to euphoria but in living it without building your whole life's plans on it. Allow yourself to enjoy the light of this moment, and don't demand that it last forever.
euphoria.practice: Go to the window and give yourself one minute of pure gladness — no phone, no plans, no promises to yourself. Schopenhauer would call it spending “ready cash”: you don't hoard it, you simply use it.

crash.text: A pendulum that swings high will swing just as far back — Schopenhauer saw in this not cruelty but mechanics. If after the high the floor seems to have been pulled out from under you, it is not proof that something is wrong with you. Schopenhauer described these swings very precisely. In The World as Will and Representation (§ 57) he noted that all excessive jubilation rests on the illusion that final satisfaction has been found — and when the illusion dissolves, a fall comes that matches the rise in strength. Then your “comedown” is not a punishment but the second half of the same wave. Schopenhauer saw real relief in understanding this mechanism: what you feel now is not a new truth about life but the swing of a pendulum, which will also pass. His advice is to keep an even keel: don't try to regain the height immediately, but let yourself come down onto solid ground.
crash.practice: Tell yourself, “This is a comedown, not a verdict.” Then do one slow, everyday thing — make tea, make the bed — the way Schopenhauer went out for his walk at the same hour each day: evenly, without hurry.

panic.text: Your heart pounds, your breath falters, the world narrows to a single point — Schopenhauer would call it the body in revolt, the will to live suddenly speaking at full volume. It is genuinely hard for you right now, and that needs to be acknowledged. Schopenhauer saw the body as “the will made visible”: the heart, the breath, the tension of the muscles are the will to live sounding the alarm. This means panic is not your weakness but an ancient force of self-preservation that has gone off too loudly. Such a wave usually rises, peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Schopenhauer also offers a way out from under the will's power: “pure contemplation,” when you stop wanting and simply look at the things around you. Even at the peak, you can shift a little in that direction — from the inner storm to the simple objects of the world.
panic.practice: Put both feet on the floor and make your out-breath longer than your in-breath. Then, like the painter Schopenhauer admired, name aloud five objects around you and the colour of each — let your eyes briefly outrank the storm.

dread.text: “Man is a metaphysical animal,” wrote Schopenhauer: the only creature that marvels at the very fact of its existence. When “what's the point of it all” and thoughts of finitude close in, you find yourself in exactly that wonder — heavy, but deeply human. Schopenhauer wrote that it is precisely the knowledge of death and suffering that most strongly drives people to philosophy; he called this the “metaphysical need” — the need to understand what it all means. In Schopenhauer's terms, your dread is not a malfunction but one of the deepest human questions, one that many before you have asked themselves. Schopenhauer offered no comforting illusions, but from this shared fragility he drew something important: since everyone faces the same thing, the most fitting way to treat one another is with compassion. In one of his late texts he even suggested seeing in everyone a “fellow sufferer.” This dread can become the place where tenderness toward yourself and others is born.
dread.practice: Schopenhauer read the Upanishads and called them the consolation of his life. Take one line that comforts you — a poem, a prayer, a friend's phrase — and read it aloud slowly, twice. Then silently wish well to one “fellow sufferer.”

fomo.text: Where is the life you're supposedly missing taking place? Schopenhauer's answer would be harsh and consoling at once: only here. The feeling that everyone is living more interesting lives and you're in the wrong place is genuinely draining. Schopenhauer described the roots of this feeling almost two hundred years ago. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he distinguished what a person “is,” what they “have,” and how they “appear” in the eyes of others — and held that we vastly overrate the last. We see other people's shop windows, but our own life from the inside, with all its humdrum days. Seen this way, the comparison is unfair from the start. Besides, Schopenhauer reminded us that the only form in which life is given to us at all is the present; past and future exist only in thought. “Somewhere out there” is a representation, while “here” is the only place you can truly be.
fomo.practice: Name three things in your “here” that don't appear in any shop window: a sound, a smell, a sensation under your palm. Schopenhauer would say this is the only place where life is given to you.

sleepless.text: “Every day is a little life: every waking and rising a little birth,” wrote Schopenhauer. At three in the morning that birth seems very far off, and everything looks huge and hopeless. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life, Schopenhauer called morning the “youth of the day” — a time of freshness and clarity — and evening its “old age.” In this light, night-time thoughts are no truer than daytime ones; it's just that the will, tired and left alone with itself, paints everything black. Schopenhauer would suggest making no decisions at night and not trying to think the thought through to the end. You can politely set it aside until morning and, in the dark, return to contemplation — to the sound of your breathing, the stillness of the room, to what simply is.
sleepless.practice: Put the thought off until morning, telling yourself, “Morning is the youth of the day; that's where I'll take it.” Then count ten slow out-breaths, listening to the stillness of the room as if it were music.

betrayal.text: Schopenhauer translated Baltasar Gracián's Pocket Oracle into German — a book of sober rules about people and trust. When trust in someone close collapses, and with it trust in your own judgment, such sobriety can turn out to be gentle. Schopenhauer believed a person's character is inborn and fundamentally unchanging: people reveal who they are gradually, and no one can see another's character in full in advance. So you weren't “stupid” to trust — you simply couldn't know what only the act revealed. Schopenhauer was sober in his conclusions too: he advised not throwing away bitter experience but keeping it as knowledge about the person. But sobriety doesn't require bitterness. He also taught that we are all manifestations of one blind will, and this lets you understand without excusing. You can protect yourself and still not turn into the one who hurt you.
betrayal.practice: Frame two sentences to yourself, like rules from the Oracle: “What I now know about this person” and “What good I still know about myself.” Say the second one aloud.

jealousy.text: People attach such importance to love affairs, Schopenhauer wrote, because what is decided in them is nothing less than the make-up of the next generation. Burning jealousy is nothing to be ashamed of: it shows how much the person means to you. In “The Metaphysics of Sexual Love,” Schopenhauer explained the force of amorous passions by the fact that what acts through us is not only personal desire but the “will to live” itself — ancient, stubborn, never asking our opinion. It follows that jealousy is the voice of that will, afraid of losing. That's why it's so strong and listens so poorly to reason. Understanding this helps you step a little to the side: you are not only your jealousy; you are also the one who sees it. From this observer's position it's easier to choose what to say and do, and what simply to live through inwardly without destroying yourself or the relationship.
jealousy.practice: Say aloud to yourself, “What's speaking in me right now is a will afraid of losing.” Name in one word what exactly you fear losing, and take a slow out-breath before saying anything to the other person.

resentment.text: Schopenhauer never made peace with his mother: for the last twenty-four years of her life they did not see each other. He knew that a long-held grudge is a load you carry for years, and that behind it there is almost always real pain. Schopenhauer helps you look at it from a new angle. He believed that people's actions follow from their character, and character hardly changes. It sounds bleak, but a liberating conclusion follows: you can stop waiting for the person who hurt you to one day become someone else and put everything right. In other words, a grudge is often held in place by this very waiting. Schopenhauer went further: he saw in all beings manifestations of one and the same blind will, which suffers and causes suffering. This understanding doesn't cancel the fact that you were in the right, but it can loosen the grip: the one who hurt you was also gripped by a force they barely understood.
resentment.practice: Ask yourself, “What am I still waiting for from this person?” Then consider what of it you could give yourself today — and do one such small thing.

heartbreak.text: Why can one person's leaving bring down an entire world? Schopenhauer thought philosophers had unfairly neglected this question and was among the first to take it seriously. If it hurts now as though everything has collapsed, that is no exaggeration. Schopenhauer gave this a remarkable explanation. In “The Metaphysics of Sexual Love” he wrote that in amorous passion it is not only the individual who acts but the “will to live” of the whole species; that's why the sufferings of love are so immense — in them, he said, something greater than the individual groans. Think this through, and the force of your pain is not a sign of weakness or “oversensitivity”: you have run into one of the most powerful forces of nature. Schopenhauer would suggest treating yourself with the same compassion he considered the basis of morality, and giving yourself respites in contemplation — in music, nature, books, where the will falls silent at least for a while.
heartbreak.practice: Choose one melody that feels close to you and listen to the end, doing nothing else. Schopenhauer believed music speaks of the very essence of pain — let it speak for you a little.

impostor.text: Schopenhauer had written his main book by thirty and waited three more decades for recognition: for a long time others' opinion of him was worlds away from what he had actually done. The sense that you're about to be exposed especially often visits conscientious people. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life, Schopenhauer distinguished three things: what a person “is,” what they “have,” and how they “appear” in others' eyes. He held that people spend an inordinate amount of energy on the third — on how they look in others' opinion — and that this is one of the chief sources of unease. Then impostor syndrome is a fear for your “appearance,” not for what you “are.” Schopenhauer advised shifting the weight onto what stays with you whatever the judgments: your knowledge, your qualities, your work. Judgments change, but what you've done already exists.
impostor.practice: Name aloud three things you have actually done or can do — facts, not judgments. Schopenhauer would say this is what you “are,” and no one else's verdict cancels it.

self_hatred.text: Schopenhauer's poodle was named Atma — “world soul” in Sanskrit — and when the dog misbehaved, its master reportedly snapped, “You human!” If your inner critic is shouting at you like that right now, know that you don't deserve this verdict. Schopenhauer believed a person's basic character is not chosen: we receive it just as we receive the colour of our eyes. This means the inner critic demands the impossible of you — to be someone else entirely. Schopenhauer offered something different: “acquired character,” that is, a calm, clear knowledge of your strengths and weaknesses, with which a person stops waging war on themselves and finds their place. And he considered the chief virtue to be “compassion” — the ability to see in another the same suffering will as in oneself. If every living being deserves compassion, there's no reason to exclude yourself from that circle.
self_hatred.practice: Imagine your inner critic saying all this to a stranger. What would you, out of compassion, say in that person's defence? Now say it to yourself — aloud or in a whisper.

helplessness.text: What is left to a person when almost nothing depends on them? Schopenhauer answered without comforting lies, but without despair either. Feeling that you can't change anything is very heavy, and it is not your fault. Schopenhauer wrote a great deal about necessity: much in life — circumstances, character, the course of events — does not bend to our wishes. But in understanding this he saw not despair but a kind of consolation: in The World as Will and Representation he noted that nothing reconciles us to an unavoidable misfortune so much as a clear grasp of its necessity — that it could not have been otherwise. So it's worth separating what is beyond your power from the tiny bit that is within it. And one more thing: powerlessness is a shared human condition. Schopenhauer suggested seeing others as “fellow sufferers,” which means you aren't alone in this either.
helplessness.practice: Draw two circles: “beyond my power” and “a little within my power.” In the second, place one very small action for today; with the first, as Schopenhauer advised, try to make peace at least for this evening.

procrastination.text: Buridan's ass, starving between two bales of hay, appears in Schopenhauer's essay on free will. Being unable to start is exhausting, and it isn't laziness: sometimes there are just too many bales. Schopenhauer would explain it through the nature of the “will”: it is constantly torn between many desires and fears, and when there are too many of them, movement gets stuck. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he makes a simple observation: all limitation makes for happiness. The narrower the circle of our concerns and possibilities, the less we are troubled and the calmer the will. Seen this way, procrastination often grows out of too wide a horizon: the task is seen whole, with all its consequences and judgments. Schopenhauer's advice is to narrow your field of vision to a single step, without asking whether it will lead to success. It's easier for the will to move when what's before it is not a mountain but one stair.
procrastination.practice: Find the smallest first step, two minutes' worth — one “stair” instead of a mountain. Do only that, and give yourself permission to stop there.

uprooted.text: His father named him Arthur because the name sounds the same in every European language: a merchant's son should feel at home anywhere. And yet being cut off from home — a move, emigration, the loss of familiar ground — is hard even for the best prepared, and it needs time. Schopenhauer knew this firsthand: as a child he left his native Danzig with his family, lived for a long time in different cities and countries, and only settled in Frankfurt in his mature years. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he insisted that what matters most for a person is what they “are” — their inner qualities — not what they “have” or where they happen to be. In this light, you have carried the most valuable things with you: your mind, your abilities, your memory, your capacity to love. This doesn't cancel your longing for the place. But the ground beneath your feet need not be only external: part of it you carry inside.
uprooted.practice: Check your “inner luggage,” as Schopenhauer might advise: silently name a skill, a habit and a memory you brought not in a suitcase but within yourself. Pick one and use it today, even for five minutes.

overload.text: “When we read, another person thinks for us,” warned Schopenhauer, though he himself devoured a huge library. If your head is already buzzing from the feed and the noise, you don't have to keep up with everything. Schopenhauer foresaw this problem long before the internet. In his essays “On Reading and Books” and “On Thinking for Oneself” he warned that whoever constantly absorbs other people's thoughts gradually forgets how to think for themselves — the head becomes a playground for other people's thoughts. So overload is not only fatigue but also a loss of your own voice. Schopenhauer valued silence and limitation: he believed our own thoughts come when room is left for them. A gentle response to overload is not willpower but a pause in which you let nothing in and allow yourself to hear what you are thinking.
overload.practice: Put your phone away and sit in silence for two minutes, letting nothing in. Schopenhauer believed our own thoughts come when room is left for them — just notice which one arrives first.

quote.text: When we read, another person thinks for us.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: Parerga and Paralipomena, “On Reading and Books” (1851)

unreality.text: How can you be sure the world is real, if all you have is your representations of it? Schopenhauer thought about this question all his life. When everything around you suddenly feels unreal, it's frightening, and hard to talk about. Schopenhauer opened his main book with the words “the world is my representation”: we know the world only through how it appears to our consciousness. In § 5 he even admitted that the boundary between dreaming and waking is not as obvious as it seems. But he also has an important addition: there is one thing we know not only as a picture but from the inside — our own body. We feel it directly, as “will” — tension, warmth, movement. It follows that even when the world seems far away, the body remains the point where you are connected to reality from within.
unreality.practice: Clench and unclench your hands; feel their warmth and weight. Tell yourself, “This is my body, and I know it from the inside” — that is how Schopenhauer described the one thing in the world given to us as more than a picture.

quote.text: Life and dreams are leaves of one and the same book.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: The World as Will and Representation, Vol. 1, § 5 (1819)

awe.text: At sixteen Schopenhauer saw Mont Blanc from Chamonix, and many years later he compared that mountain, almost always veiled in cloud, to the melancholy of genius. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious experience. Schopenhauer described it in detail under the name of “the sublime.” When we see a storm, mountains, a starry sky, we feel tiny before the forces of nature. But at the same time, he wrote, something else awakens in us: the “pure subject of knowing,” which calmly contemplates all this grandeur and is not afraid. Fear for oneself recedes, and we simply look. In other words, awe is one of those rare moments when the will in you falls silent and you become pure seeing. Schopenhauer considered such moments the best that life offers: in them, suffering and desire let go for a while. You don't need to do anything with it — just stay in it.
awe.practice: Go outside or to a window and find the biggest thing in view: the sky, a tree, a building. Look at it for a minute, feeling your smallness and at the same time the calm spectator inside, whom Schopenhauer called the pure subject of knowing.

relief.text: “We do not feel the health of our whole body, only the small spot where the shoe pinches,” wrote Schopenhauer. When the shoe finally comes off, relief arrives — warm and quiet, and worth savouring. Schopenhauer gave it special significance. He believed we feel suffering directly and sharply, while well-being is felt only as the absence of suffering. It sounds pessimistic, but a lovely conclusion follows: relief is the moment when we actually notice our happiness. Usually health, peace and safety are as invisible as air; only when the weight lifts do we feel how much we have. Think this through, and relief is a rare chance to see the value of the ordinary. Schopenhauer rated freedom from pain above the pursuit of pleasures, and that is exactly what you're experiencing now. Allow yourself simply to breathe out.
relief.practice: Take a slow out-breath, as if taking off a tight shoe. Name one ordinary thing you value more now than yesterday, and hold it in your mind for a moment.

calm.text: In his last years Schopenhauer began every day alike: cold water, coffee, work till noon, lunch, a long walk with his poodle. The calm you feel now he prized above almost everything — it's good simply to rest in it. Schopenhauer described it in his theory of contemplation. Usually, he wrote, we live under the sway of the “will” and spin like Ixion on his wheel in the Greek myth — with no respite from desires and fears. But there are moments when we look at the world without self-interest: at a sunset, at water, at the face of a sleeping child. Then, in his words, Ixion's wheel stands still, and a sabbath arrives, a respite from the penal servitude of willing. Then your calm is neither emptiness nor laziness but one of the best states available to a human being. Schopenhauer would not urge you to use it or prolong it by effort — only to notice it and cherish it.
calm.practice: Notice where in your body this calm lives. Stay with it for a minute, adding nothing — the way Schopenhauer taught us to look at a sunset: without trying to hold on to it.

inspiration.text: Schopenhauer carried a notebook and jotted thoughts down right in the middle of his walks: he knew a good thought comes for a moment and leaves just as fast. If inspiration has caught you now, it's worth receiving with gratitude. Schopenhauer believed the best thoughts and images come when we are freed for a while from personal concerns and begin to look at things “objectively” — without asking what they give us personally. He called this ability the essence of genius, but saw its seeds in everyone. In the essay “On Thinking for Oneself” he noted that your own thoughts cannot be summoned on command: they come by themselves when room is left for them. This means inspiration is your pure view of the world, freed from the bustle. Schopenhauer would advise you not to let it slip: write it down while it's here, and don't measure it by usefulness or by others' judgments.
inspiration.practice: Do as Schopenhauer did on his walks: write down what came to you right now, in any form — words, a sketch, a list — without editing. Judge its usefulness later.

schadenfreude.text: “The most devilish trait of human nature” — that is what Schopenhauer, in On the Basis of Morality, called joy at another's misfortune: the direct opposite of compassion. Noticing it in yourself is unpleasant, but his own philosophy explains where it comes from. Each of us, for Schopenhauer, carries an insatiable will and a constant lack. Here is what follows: when your own burden is heavy, someone else's failure makes it lighter for a moment — “I'm not the only one.” Schadenfreude then speaks above all of your own pain. And then Schopenhauer suggests an important step: to see that the one who stumbled suffers from the very same will as you. The very ability to notice schadenfreude in yourself is already the beginning of compassion, not a reason to punish yourself.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: which pain of my own quieted for a second at someone else's failure? Name it in a word or two — and wish the one who stumbled the same relief you want for yourself.

contempt.text: Schopenhauer called Hegel a “flat, witless charlatan” and hardly minced his words. When someone's foolishness, cruelty or baseness stirs a cold contempt in you, he would understand better than most. Schopenhauer knew this feeling himself: he made no secret of his contempt for fashionable philosophers and for “the crowd.” But in Parerga and Paralipomena he proposed a remedy that can soften even it. People, he wrote, should address one another as “fellow sufferers.” Such an address reminds us that each person carries the same blind will — desire, lack, fear — and that their weaknesses grew from the same soil as ours. Seen this way, contempt divides people into “higher” and “lower,” while compassion sees a shared plight. This doesn't cancel your judgment of the action. But it lets you avoid carrying a coldness that chills you yourself first of all.
contempt.practice: Silently address this person the way Schopenhauer suggested: “fellow sufferer.” Say it to yourself twice and imagine one burden they may be carrying.

disgust.text: There are things, Schopenhauer thought, that cannot even be painted in a way that lets us look at them calmly. Disgust is very bodily: you want to turn away, draw back, wall yourself off. Schopenhauer spoke of it in his theory of art. The beautiful, in his view, allows us to stop wanting for a while and simply contemplate. The disgusting, on the contrary, immediately wakes the will — the body says a sharp “no,” and calm contemplation becomes impossible. That's why disgust is so hard to “think your way out of”: it happens before reasoning does. In this light, there's no need to be ashamed of it — it's a protective reaction of the will, looking out for you. If the disgust is directed at yourself, Schopenhauer would remind you that the will living in you is the same as in all beings. There is no special vileness in you: there is human nature, equally imperfect in everyone.
disgust.practice: Step back from whatever disgusts you and take a few slow out-breaths. Then shift your gaze to something you can look at calmly, and ask yourself: what is my “no” protecting right now?

revenge.text: What exactly does the one who takes revenge get? Schopenhauer asked this without moralizing, almost like an accountant. If you're seething with the urge to get even, there is almost always real pain behind it. Schopenhauer drew an important distinction. Punishment, he wrote, looks to the future: its purpose is to protect, to prevent new harm. Revenge looks to the past, and the past cannot be changed. So revenge, in his view, cannot give what is expected of it: what was done will not be undone, and new pain only multiplies the suffering in a world already overflowing with it. Schopenhauer added a deeper thought: the one who causes pain and the one who suffers are manifestations of one and the same will, so in wounding another the will wounds itself. Better, then, to turn the force now boiling inside toward the future: how to protect yourself and keep this from happening again.
revenge.practice: Turn your gaze around, as Schopenhauer advised — from the past to the future. Silently name one step that would protect you from a repeat and harm no one.

anger_at_loved.text: Johanna Schopenhauer wrote to her son that she loved him but couldn't live under one roof with him — hard to find a more honest picture of anger at loved ones. Loving someone and still lashing out is one of the most painful feelings. Schopenhauer would explain it this way: the will — our constant striving — is invested most heavily precisely in those close to us. From them we want the most: understanding, care, for them to be different. Where desire is stronger, the collision with reality hurts more. Schopenhauer considered a person's character almost unchangeable, and in the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he advised accepting people as they are rather than being angry with them for their nature. It follows that anger often flares up in the place of an expectation that “they should be different.” There's no need to be ashamed of it. But it's worth noticing which expectation has just collided with who the person really is.
anger_at_loved.practice: Before going on with the conversation, tell your loved one, “I need five minutes.” Step out, breathe, and ask yourself which expectation — “they should be different” — has just collided with who they are.

ambivalence.text: One of Schopenhauer's best-known stories is about little animals who can't settle down side by side. Loving someone close and being unable to stand them at the same time is an almost inevitable side of closeness. Schopenhauer told of this in his famous parable of the porcupines in Parerga and Paralipomena. On a cold winter's day the porcupines huddle together for warmth, but prick each other with their quills and move apart. The cold drives them together again, the quills wound again, and so they are tossed back and forth until they find a moderate distance at which they can both keep warm and not prick each other too much. In other words, your mixed feelings are a natural consequence of closeness: the closer people are, the stronger both the warmth and the pricks. You don't have to choose which feeling is the “real” one. You can look for your own distance — the one at which there is more warmth than pain.
ambivalence.practice: Picture this person in a room and move their chair in your mind — closer, further. At what distance is there more warmth than pricking? That is your “moderate distance” for today.

guilty_relief.text: If compassion means feeling another's pain as your own, as Schopenhauer believed, then the end of that pain becomes partly yours too. Relief after a loved one's long illness and death, after a departure or a breakup, often frightens people: how can you feel this alongside grief? Schopenhauer helps you understand why it's natural. He believed we feel suffering directly and sharply, while satisfaction is felt only as the ending of pain. Relief is exactly such an ending: long strain, fear, sleepless nights finally let go. It is not joy at the loss but a body and soul breathing out for the first time in a long while. And if your loved one suffered greatly, relief can also be a form of compassion — what Schopenhauer considered the basis of love: you felt their pain as your own, and now it has ended. Think this through, and relief and love do not contradict each other.
guilty_relief.practice: Allow yourself one slow out-breath — the one you haven't taken in months — and tell yourself, “It was very hard for me.” There's nothing more you need to prove.

indifference.text: Why does one piece of news pierce you while another passes by? For Schopenhauer this is one of ethics' great puzzles. When an event “should” move you but inside it's empty, it's easy to suspect yourself of callousness. Schopenhauer called compassion “the great mystery of ethics.” What's surprising is not that we are sometimes indifferent but that another's pain can become ours at all. Usually, in his view, we live under the “veil of Maya” — we see the world divided into separate beings, where the other is simply “not me.” Compassion happens when this veil becomes transparent for a moment. Then you can't order yourself to feel compassion, and the absence of feeling is not a verdict. It may mean tiredness, being overloaded with your own pain, or that the event hasn't yet become real to you. Compassion can't be forced, but you can leave room for it — for example, by imagining not the event in general but one particular person.
indifference.practice: Instead of thinking about the event as a whole, picture one particular person within it — their face, their morning. Notice whether the “veil of Maya” has lifted even slightly.

escape.text: At seventeen Schopenhauer worked in a Hamburg merchant's office and secretly read books under his desk — that's how badly he wanted to drop everything. The urge to escape from a job, a city, a role can be very strong. Two years later, after his father's death, he finally resolved to leave for study and philosophy. But he also warned that when we change places, we take ourselves along. The will — our restless striving — travels with us to any city. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he wrote that what matters most for happiness is what a person is in themselves, not what they have or how they look in others' eyes. This means you can hear the urge to escape as a question: what am I myself missing — an occupation, quiet, meaning? Sometimes a change of circumstances is needed, sometimes a change within.
escape.practice: Imagine yourself already there, where you want to escape to — on the first evening. What are you doing? Find a small form of that activity that's possible right here, and give it ten minutes today.

forbidden_attraction.text: Who decided you'd be drawn to this person? Schopenhauer would answer: not you — at least not the part of you that decides. Such attraction often takes you by surprise: you decided nothing, yet the feeling is here. Schopenhauer described this as the will's main characteristic. In the second volume of The World as Will and Representation he compared the relationship between will and intellect to a strong blind man carrying on his shoulders a lame man who can see. The will wants first; the intellect learns of its desires afterwards and is often surprised by them itself. In Schopenhauer's terms, an attraction that's “not allowed” is neither a decision nor evidence of your depravity, but a movement of the will that your consciousness has simply received news of. Schopenhauer urged neither submitting to the will nor being ashamed of it. He proposed understanding and contemplating. You can calmly look at this desire: what is it seeking, which lack is it answering?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Say silently, like an observer: “The will in me reaches toward… because it lacks…”. Draw no conclusions and don't rush to act — just look at what comes out.

social_anxiety.text: Schopenhauer dined at a shared table in a Frankfurt hotel and, the story goes, laid a gold coin before him — for the poor, should the officers ever talk of anything but horses and women. For many of us, any shared table turns into an exam. Schopenhauer devoted part of the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life to the fear of being judged. He distinguished three sources of our well-being: what a person is, what they have, and how they appear in others' eyes. And he held that people greatly overrate the third — others' opinion. As he observed, a huge share of our anxieties concerns what others will think, although their thoughts about us are usually fleeting: everyone is busy with their own will and their own worries. Seen this way, your nervousness is understandable, but its object is much smaller than it seems. Schopenhauer advised gradually shifting the weight from others' gaze to what you yourself are. This doesn't require courage all at once — only a habit of noticing.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, choose one quality you value in yourself regardless of how the conversation goes, and put your hand in your pocket as if gripping Schopenhauer's coin: this is yours, and the stakes have nothing to do with it.

uncertainty.text: Time, Schopenhauer wrote, is like a revolving sphere, and the present is the point where it touches the plane: without extension, yet the only place the sphere rests. When the future is unclear, the will, wanting to know how it all ends, has a hard time. Schopenhauer stressed that future and past exist only in our concepts, while what is truly given is only the present: the one form in which life appears to us at all. Yet we constantly live where we are not — in an imagined “later.” In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he offered the rule “limitation makes for happiness”: the narrower the circle of our concerns, the fewer reasons for anxiety. In this light, you needn't try to take in all possible outcomes at once; you can narrow your gaze to what is happening today and what can be done now. The uncertainty won't disappear, but it will stop filling all of your time.
uncertainty.practice: Walk slowly for five minutes, noticing each touch of your foot on the ground — the way Schopenhauer's sphere touches the plane at a single point. With each step, say to yourself: “here.”

waiting.text: What makes time thick as tar? Schopenhauer noticed that hours fly when we are occupied and crawl when we merely wait. If everything inside is straining toward a moment that just won't come, it is genuinely hard. For Schopenhauer this is an almost pure picture of the will — a striving that reaches forward and cannot settle. But he also knew a state in which this pull lets go for a while. When we give ourselves entirely to contemplation — of a cloud, a melody, a painting — we stop being only a wanting creature and become simply a looking one. Schopenhauer described this as a “Sabbath” — a day of rest from the penal servitude of the will. So waiting needn't be overcome by force. For a few minutes you can switch from “when will it happen” to “what do I see or hear right now.” The waiting will remain, but you'll have little islands of respite.
waiting.practice: Choose one thing near you — a sound, a light, an object — and for two minutes take it in as if it were the only thing happening. Schopenhauer would call it a small “Sabbath” in the middle of waiting.

quote.text: We keep the Sabbath of the penal servitude of willing; the wheel of Ixion stands still.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: The World as Will and Representation, Vol. 1, § 38 (1819)

regret.text: Schopenhauer compared life to embroidery: in the first half we see the right side, in the second the reverse, where you can see how the threads are joined. When “if only I had…” comes back again, you are looking at the reverse — and it hurts. We really do what we want, but what exactly we want follows from our character and the circumstances of that moment. It follows that your choice back then was an expression of who you were and what you knew then, not random foolishness. Schopenhauer also spoke of “acquired character” — the knowledge of ourselves we accumulate through experience, including through mistakes. Regret then becomes part of that knowledge: it tells you what truly matters to you rather than proving that you're bad.
regret.practice: Say aloud, “Back then I was who I was and knew what I knew.” Then name one thread this mistake revealed on the reverse side: what truly matters to you.

quote.text: Man can do what he wills but he cannot will what he wills.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: On the Freedom of the Will (1839)

longing.text: Why can the absence of one particular person feel almost like a presence? Schopenhauer understood this double feeling — and if you miss someone that much right now, he wouldn't hurry you. On the one hand, the will won't let go: it wants precisely this person, and no one else will do. On the other, he wrote about the magic that memory casts over the past and the distant. When we remember, we see the image without the bustle of desires and anxieties that accompanied reality, and so it shines especially brightly. In other words, your longing is made of two threads: a real lack, and this soft light of memory. The first you can simply acknowledge — it speaks of the depth of the bond. The second you can cherish: there is something of contemplation in it, in which pain briefly becomes beauty.
longing.practice: Close your eyes and recreate one scene with this person in three or four details — a colour, a sound, a gesture. Look at it like a painting, in the contemplation Schopenhauer spoke of: not demanding, just seeing.

world_pain.text: Schopenhauer was among the first European philosophers to include animals in the circle of compassion. When news of war, injustice and other people's grief becomes unbearable, it shows how wide your own circle is. Schopenhauer was perhaps the most honest philosopher of suffering: he didn't deny that there is an enormous amount of it in the world. But he considered the main answer to it to be compassion — the ability to feel another's pain as your own. He saw this not as weakness but as the foundation of all morality. Think this through, and your pain for the world is the very best thing Schopenhauer found in human beings. Yet he also knew the danger of drowning. That is why, alongside compassion, he placed art and contemplation — minutes when the will falls silent and you can recover your strength. Protecting such minutes is not an escape from the world but a condition for your fellow-feeling not to run dry.
world_pain.practice: Do one small thing out of compassion — for someone near you, for people far away or for an animal. Then give yourself five minutes of music or silence, so your fellow-feeling has somewhere to draw strength from.

quote.text: Boundless compassion for all living beings is the firmest and surest guarantee of pure moral conduct.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

rejection.text: The Royal Danish Academy refused a prize to Schopenhauer's treatise on morality — even though he was the only entrant in the competition. Rejection wounds: the will in each of us wants to be accepted. Schopenhauer, however, helps us look at it from another side. He believed that each person's choice flows from their own character and their own will — and that will can't be argued with. When you are rejected, what decides is someone else's make-up, their inclinations and lacks, which you didn't choose and can't change. This doesn't always say anything about your worth. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life Schopenhauer insisted that what matters most is what a person is in themselves, not how others rate them. Then a refusal is an event that hurts to live through, but not a verdict on who you are.
rejection.practice: Call or message someone who has known and valued you for a long time — just to talk. Schopenhauer would say that what you “are” isn't decided by one person's choice, and sometimes it helps to hear that in another voice.

abandonment.text: What can you lean on if anything you lean on might, it seems, leave at any moment? Schopenhauer thought about this seriously. The fear of being abandoned can be very old and very deep, and nobody makes it up. Schopenhauer knew ruptures firsthand: after a bitter quarrel with his mother he didn't see her for many years. His philosophy explains why this fear is so strong: the will clings to what is dear to it and senses loss long before it happens. Schopenhauer advised cultivating what he called inner wealth — interests, thoughts, the ability to find support in yourself. This doesn't mean giving up closeness or loving less. Rather, it means that if you lean not only on another person, the fear of loss stops being a matter of survival. This means inner wealth is not a wall but a floor under your feet.
abandonment.practice: Choose one activity that fills you even when you're alone — Schopenhauer would call it part of your “inner wealth” — and give it at least ten minutes today.

unrequited.text: At forty-three Schopenhauer gave young Flora Weiss a bunch of grapes — and she, as she later recalled, quietly dropped them into the water behind her. Philosophers know unrequited love too, and its pain can feel out of proportion to anything else. In “The Metaphysics of Sexual Love,” Schopenhauer explained why. He believed that in intense love it is not only the individual who speaks but something much greater — the will to live itself, which he called “the genius of the species.” That's why passion feels like destiny, and its failure like a catastrophe: something ancient and immense is striving through one person. In Schopenhauer's terms, the depth of your pain is neither exaggeration nor weakness of character; this is how a force greater than any of us works. Schopenhauer promised no quick consolation, but he pointed to a respite — art, music, contemplation. In them the pain doesn't vanish, but for a while it stops being only yours and becomes something all humans share.
unrequited.practice: Find a poem or song about unrequited love and read or listen to it slowly. Schopenhauer would say: for a minute your pain becomes everyone's — a great many people before you have suffered over this.

humiliation.text: In Schopenhauer's Germany people were still called out to duels over insults, as if honour could be taken away by one rude word. Humiliation wounds deeply because it strikes at your dignity — and Schopenhauer didn't dispute that. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life, Schopenhauer took apart what people call honour. He scathingly mocked the “knightly” code by which an insulted person supposedly becomes covered in disgrace until they take revenge. Schopenhauer considered this absurd: rudeness and insult speak of the one who commits them, not of the one they strike. A person's true worth, in his view, lies in what they are, not in others' opinion, which may be foolish, malicious or hasty. Here is what follows: you were hurt, and that deserves to be acknowledged, but your dignity does not pass into the hands of the one who tried to take it away.
humiliation.practice: Stand up straight, plant your feet firmly and take three slow breaths. Tell yourself, “This act speaks about them; about me it says only that I was hurt.” Schopenhauer would consider this the only sensible duel.

body_shame.text: Teeth, throat and stomach are hunger made flesh, Schopenhauer wrote, and grasping hands and quick feet are strivings made flesh. If your own body has seemed wrong to you for years, there are almost always other people's gazes and comparisons behind it. For Schopenhauer the body is not an object we carry around but our will made visible: the way life in us shows itself outwardly. We know our body in two ways — from the inside, as feeling, movement and desire, and from the outside, as an image among other images. Shame lives almost entirely in the second way — in the view from outside, often someone else's. In this light, you can return to the first: your body is what you live with, breathe with, feel with, not a picture to be graded. Schopenhauer in general advised against giving others' opinions power over what you are.
body_shame.practice: Close your eyes for a minute and feel your body from the inside — breath, warmth, support: this is the first, inner knowledge of it that Schopenhauer wrote about. Notice what it is like without a mirror.

illness.text: “Nine-tenths of our happiness depend on health,” Schopenhauer wrote, and there's not a drop of condescension toward the sick in that phrase. When your body lets you down, a sense of injustice and loneliness is added to the pain. Schopenhauer was one of the few philosophers who didn't try to prettify suffering. He considered it the basic fabric of life, not a punishment, a mistake or a personal failure. So illness is not a sign that you did something wrong: it is part of the common human lot, shared by countless beings. Schopenhauer valued health highly and understood how much it means — so he would never say illness is “for the best.” But he knew that even on hard days there can be minutes when the will falls quiet: music, the view from a window, quiet contemplation. They don't heal, but they offer a respite, and you can allow yourself that.
illness.practice: Allow yourself a couple of minutes of contemplation: find something pleasant to look at — light on the wall, a branch outside the window — or something pleasant to hear. For that time, let the one who perceives in you outrank the one who is ill.

pride.text: Schopenhauer was so sure of his work that in the preface to its second edition he stated plainly that he was handing it over not to his contemporaries but to mankind. If you're pleased with what you've done right now, that is a good and well-earned feeling. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life, Schopenhauer drew a distinction that helps you enjoy it without needless doubts. Pride, he wrote, is an inner conviction of one's own worth in some respect, while vanity is the desire to awaken such a conviction in others. Pride is calm and needs no audience; vanity is noisy and depends on others' approval. It follows that pride in work well done is one of those goods that lie within yourself — and these Schopenhauer ranked above all others. There's no need to be ashamed of it, nor to prove it to anyone. You can simply know: I did this, and I did it well.
pride.practice: Say to yourself, silently, with no witnesses: “I did this.” Sit in silence with the feeling for a minute, sharing it with no one — Schopenhauer would call it pride that needs no audience.

melancholy.text: A melody in a minor key can be beautiful — and Schopenhauer believed this holds the key to the state you're in now, where sadness is somehow good. Schopenhauer understood this like no one else. He believed that music expresses not this or that particular sorrow but sorrow itself, its essence — and so, listening to a sad melody, we live through it as if without our own pain. Melancholy is similar: the sadness is there, but it doesn't demand or grasp; it contemplates. In other words, melancholy is a rare case in which the will falls quiet but the feeling remains. Schopenhauer, following Aristotle, noted that deep, creative natures are prone to melancholy. That doesn't mean it's required. But if it has come, there's no need to hurry it away — you can stay in it and see the world a little more clearly.
melancholy.practice: Put on one slow piece in a minor key and listen to it by the window, doing nothing else. Schopenhauer would say the music is grieving for you now — notice how the sadness in it grows softer.
